data.title: Trump official seeks $50 billion for air traffic control after outage
data.description:
By David Shepardson

The Trump administration boosted its request for air traffic control funding to $50 billion late Friday after a communications issue forced a nationwide groundstop that halted thousands of flights for hours.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and the White House earlier on Friday asked for $30.1 billion to upgrade the United States' aging airports and air traffic control system.

"This is an emergency," Duffy said. "What's more important than having an air traffic control system that actually works?"

The issue impacted the FAA's en route centers that handle traffic between airports. But the Republican-led Senate Commerce Committee said the incident highlights the need to prioritize modernizing those centers over other projects and noted Congress approved $1.9 billion to replace outdated en route centers.

The world's most complex airspace has experienced a series of events in recent years that have disrupted flights and risked safety. In January 2025, a midair collision at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport killed 67 people.

Congress already approved $12.5 billion over five years in July 2025 to upgrade air traffic control and increase the hiring of controllers following complaints about airport ​congestion, flight delays and technology ​problems.

The request from White House Office of Management and Budget Director Russell Vought and Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy seeks $10.1 billion for air traffic control modernization, including $7.2 billion for a common automation platform and controller workstations and $2 billion for cloud computing.

"This investment is critical to complete the modernization of our national airspace - delivering a resilient telecommunications backbone for air traffic controllers, modern hardware and software, state-of-the-art control towers, and world-class airport infrastructure," Duffy and Vought wrote to lawmakers asking for swift action.

Major airlines including American Airlines , Delta Air Lines , United Airlines and Southwest Airlines have expressed support for the request.

The $30.1 billion request also includes $2 billion to replace and improve Federal Aviation Administration air traffic control towers and $18 billion for airport-related projects including $10 billion to modernize or replace aging terminals.

The FAA relies on decades-old ​computers as well as replacement parts bought through auction websites. Last week, it said it would replace by the end of 2028 floppy disks used for weather and other critical information at more than 400 air traffic control facilities.

Vought and Duffy in their letter said the FAA has replaced 68% of legacy copper telecommunications network with high-speed fiber infrastructure.

The administration has called for the Republican-led Congress to approve funding in the final weeks of the year. Democrats are set to take control of Congress in January.

In September, the dual failures of a circuit at a Philadelphia ​air traffic facility and the ​accidental severing of a ⁠fiber-optic cable in New Jersey by a construction crew led to thousands of flights across the densely populated Northeast being delayed or canceled.

data.title: Airlines aim to get passengers on their way as ground stop lifted
data.description:
Key points:
  • A nationwide ground stop at all US airports that began around 4p ET and ended around 8p ET is over, but the impact on stranded passengers could take days to fix.
  • JetBlue Airways said it was cancelling all flights scheduled for Friday night, except for Europe-bound departures. 
  • United Airlines said it is " cancelling a significant number of Friday evening flights" and American Airlines said that "teams across American are working to safely get additional flights moving and customers on their way as conditions allow." Earlier, the airline said it will "be all hands on deck across American to get customers on their way as soon as possible."
  • While the ground stop was in effect, Southwest said it was "making operational adjustments across our network in compliance with the nationwide groundstop."
  • All airlines appear to be waiving change fees. 
  • Around 1.5 million people are impacted by flight cancellations, based on analysis from Cirium.

data.title: Biocure Technology Inc. Provides Update on Transaction to Acquire Glorious Success Limited
data.description:
(TheNewswire)

VANCOUVER, British Columbia – TheNewswire - November 13, 2026 - Biocure Technology Inc. (“CURE” or the “Company”) (CSE: CURE) announces, further to its press release dated August 12, 2026, that it has entered into an amendment dated November 10, 2026 (the “Amendment”) to the definitive share exchange agreement dated August 11, 2026 (the “Share Exchange Agreement”) with Glorious Success Limited (“GSL”) pursuant to which Company will acquire all of the issued and outstanding securities of GSL (the “Transaction”).

The Amendment adjust the aggregate consideration due for the currently outstanding shares of GSL (the “GSL Shares”) from 12,459,091 shares of CURE following completion of the Transaction (the “Resulting Issuer”) to 11,325,464 shares of the Resulting Issuer. In addition the Amendment extends the outside date for completion of the Transaction and related concurrent financing from December 31, 2026 to January 31, 2027. All other terms of the Transaction remain the same.

GSL is a Hong Kong holding company and the sole shareholder of Idea Paragon Inc., a South Korea-based mixed martial arts (MMA) promotion and sports media company operating as Black Combat.

Trading in the common shares of the Company is currently halted in accordance with the policies of the CSE and will remain halted until such time as all required documentation in connection with the Transaction has been filed with and accepted by the CSE and permission to resume trading has been obtained from the CSE.

Transaction Summary

Pursuant to the Share Exchange Agreement as amended by the Amendment, the Company will consolidate its existing share capital on the basis of a ratio determined by the price of GSL securities in the Private Placement (as defined below) divided by a deemed value of $0.134 (the “Consolidation”), currently expected to result in a consolidation ratio equal to approximately 16.42 old shares for one new common share (the “Resulting Issuer Shares”). As outlined above, pursuant to the Amendment, as consideration for the currently outstanding shares of GSL (the “GSL Shares”), the Company will issue an aggregate of 11,325,464 Resulting Issuer Shares.

No finder’s fees are payable in connection with the Transaction. Each of Collin Kim, Konstantin Lichtenwald and Steven Pearce will be entitled to receive a bonus for their services to the Company in association with the Transaction, equivalent to 250,000 Resulting Issuer Shares each.

The Transaction remains subject to a number of terms and conditions, including, but not limited to, the completion of additional due diligence, the completion of the Consolidation, the completion of the Private Placement as further described below, the completion of the Debt Settlement as further described below, the approval of the shareholders of the Company, and the approval of the CSE and other applicable regulatory authorities.

Private Placement

Pursuant to the Share Exchange Agreement, it is a condition of the Transaction that GSL complete a private placement for aggregate gross proceeds of at least $3,090,000 at a price of $2.20 per GSL Share (the “Private Placement”). GSL Shares issuable pursuant to the Private Placement will be exchanged for Resulting Issuer Shares on a one for one basis.

Cash finder’s fees of 8% of the proceeds raised are expected to be payable in connection with the Private Placement.

The Resulting Issuer intends to use the net proceeds of the private placement to fund the Transaction, to develop its business and for working capital.

This news release does not constitute an offer to sell and is not a solicitation of an offer to buy any securities in the United States. The securities of the Company and GSL have not been and will not be registered under the United States Securities Act of 1933, as amended (the “U.S. Securities Act”) or any state securities laws and may not be offered or sold within the United States or to U.S. Persons unless registered under the U.S. Securities Act and applicable state securities laws unless pursuant to an exemption from such registration.

Debt Settlement

As conditions of the Transaction, the Company intends to settle approximately $300,000 in debt (the “Debt Settlement" owed to various parties through the issuance of pre-Consolidation common shares of the Company at a price of $0.134 per share (the “Settlement Shares”), subject to the approval of the CSE. Portions of the indebtedness are expected to be settled with members of the Company’s management team and will constitute a “related party transaction” as defined in MI 61-101. The Settlement Shares will be subject to applicable resale restrictions under securities laws.

Board of Directors of Resulting Issuer

Upon completion of the Transaction, the board and management of the Resulting Issuer shall be reconstituted to comprise:

Pyounghwa Park – Director and Chief Executive Officer

Prior to founding Black Combat, Mr. Park was the Director and Founder of Chromatic Film, where he produced a range of mixed martial arts documentaries that laid the creative foundation for Black Combat’s unique brand identity. In addition to his executive role, Mr. Park is also a professional mixed martial arts fighter within the Black Combat Universe, currently holding the Underground King Title. His personal success in the ring and the popularity of his matches were pivotal in the creation and early growth of the organization.

Jongeon Lim – Director and President

Mr. Lim brings a multidisciplinary background in healthcare, corporate leadership, and media entrepreneurship. Prior to co-founding Black Combat, Mr. Lim served as CEO of ADM Korea Inc., a publicly listed company on the KOSDAQ, and practiced medicine at Mojelim, one of Korea’s leading plastic surgery clinics. His passion for marketing and strategic business development played a central role in launching Black Combat alongside Mr. Park. In his current capacity, Mr. Lim is responsible for strategic partnerships and business development, spearheading collaborations with companies such as My Music Tastes and Sidus to amplify the brand’s reach. He also leads investor relations and contributes medical expertise to the organization, ensuring the well-being and performance readiness of its athletes

Jong Yun Choi – Director

Mr. Choi holds a degree in Business from Oklahoma State University and previously worked as a valuation specialist at Yuanta Korea. He is currently the CEO of DEA TI Co., a Kosdaq-listed company in Korea, as well as the CEO of The Nice Music Group, a hip-hop label. Leveraging his experience in both venture capital and large-scale enterprises, he oversees business transactions to ensure corporate transparency.

Anthony Wong – Director

Mr. Wong is an accomplished senior executive and board director with extensive experience in corporate governance, financial oversight, strategic transactions, and international business across publicly listed companies in Canada, Singapore, and Hong Kong. Mr. Wong is a Member of the Chartered Professional Accountants of Canada and the Institute of Chartered Accountants of British Columbia.

Sang Goo (Collin) Kim – Director

Mr. Kim has been involved in various mineral projects bringing together Canadian and major Korean companies as well as involved in several listing transactions where Korean companies were successfully listed in the Canadian stock exchanges. Mr. Kim is a Vice President for Columbia Capital Inc. since 2008 and has been a director of First Atlantic Nickel Corp., a Canadian junior exploration company since 2015 until his recent resignation in May 2025. He worked for Hanwha Corp. one of Korean business conglomerates for 16 years including five years as a Chief Representative of Hanwha’s Jakarta office, dedicating himself to trading business.

Konstantin Lichtenwald – Chief Financial Officer

Mr. Lichtenwald is a Canadian CPA, CGA and an ACCA in the UK and has over 17 years of corporate finance experience, including experience in accounting, financial management, compliance, M&A, reverse takeovers and initial public offerings. He has lived and worked in multiple jurisdictions including Germany, Australia, USA and Canada. He is a director of a number of private and publicly listed companies in Canada. Mr. Lichtenwald holds a Bachelor of Business from Pforzheim University located in Germany.

Shareholder Meeting

Approval for the Transaction, including the Consolidation, will be sought from the Company’s shareholders at an annual and special meeting to be held on December 16, 2026 (the “Meeting”).

Name Change

Upon completion of the Transaction, the Company intends to change its name to “Black Combat Universe Inc.” or an alternate name selected by the parties, and the CSE will assign a new trading symbol for the Resulting Issuer.

Information Concerning GSL

Black Combat 17 is going to be held at Gocheok Sky Dome (21,000 audiences capacity) and tickets has been completely sold-out in 55 minutes. Main event is Kim Jae-Woong (“Fighting God”, current Champion)) and former UFC Fighter, Kang Kyung-Ho (“Mr. Perfect”). Choo Sung-hoon (aka Akiyama Yoshihiro, “Sexyama”) and Chris Leben (“The Crippler”)’s legendary retirement match will be a co-main event of November 21st.

Black Combat recently dropped 6 theme-songs with collaboration of Korean hiphop artists, BewhY, Jimmy Paige, JUSTHIS, Potty Monkey and Pull Up 22. They will be on the half-time show of Black Combat 17 as well.

Black Cup Final “USA Vs Mongolia” is expected to be held at Ulaanbaatar, a capital of Mongolia in December 2026. According to Mongolian OTT “VOO”, Black Combat is famous in nation-wide and they expect Black Cup Final to be their biggest year-end event. Black Cup 2026 started as round of 8, but in 2027 it will be a round of 16: participating countries will be revealed on 2027 Black Combat contents.

data.title: U.S. Flights Resume After FAA Lifts Nationwide Ground Stop, But Delays Persist
data.description:
WASHINGTON (dpa-AFX) - Air travel across the United States began returning to normal after the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) lifted a nationwide ground stop that had halted domestic departures for more than four hours following a major telecommunications outage.

The unprecedented disruption affected airports across the country, leaving thousands of flights delayed or canceled and creating widespread uncertainty for airlines, passengers and airport operators. The outage impacted communications at multiple Air Route Traffic Control Centers, prompting the FAA to temporarily stop departing flights nationwide while technicians worked to identify and resolve the issue.

'The FAA issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following communication issues impacting multiple Air Route Traffic Control Centers,' the agency said, adding that its technicians were investigating the source of the disruption.

Following restoration of critical communications systems, the FAA lifted the ground stop and authorized flights to resume operations. However, aviation authorities warned that delays and schedule disruptions are expected to continue as airlines work through significant backlogs and reposition aircraft and crews.

The impact extended beyond the United States, with U.S.-bound flights departing from major airports across the Asia-Pacific region also affected by the temporary halt. Airlines operating transpacific routes were forced to adjust schedules, delay departures or hold aircraft pending further guidance from U.S. authorities.

The disruption underscores the aviation sector's reliance on stable communications infrastructure, as even brief outages can ripple through the highly interconnected air traffic system. Industry observers noted that recovery from large-scale ground stops often takes several hours after restrictions are lifted, particularly at major airline hubs.

While flight operations have resumed, passengers are being advised to check the status of their flights before heading to the airport, as carriers continue to manage delays and cancellations caused by the outage.

The FAA said it will continue investigating the telecommunications issue and provide further updates as more information becomes available.

How to Make the Most of Rising Bond Yields — Barron's
data.description:
Mary Ellen Stanek, Baird's chief investment officer emeritus, sees value in financial-company bonds, higher-quality municipals.

By Debbie Carlson

Bonds offer investors some of the most attractive yields in decades on a nominal and an inflation-adjusted basis, says Mary Ellen Stanek, managing director and chief investment officer emeritus at Milwaukee-based Baird Advisors.

With 47 years of fixed-income investment management experience under her belt, Stanek should know.

Bonds may experience volatility due to uncertainty about inflation, the interest-rate outlook, and other macroeconomic issues, but investors shouldn't be afraid to lock in current yields, she says.

Baird manages $195 billion across 10 taxable and municipal bond funds, all rated highly by Morningstar. Stanek is a named portfolio manager on the firm's five taxable bond funds. She spoke with Barron's on Oct. 20 and Nov. 3 about her economic and bond market outlook and corporate and municipal credits that the Baird team likes now.

An edited version of the conversation follows.

Barron's: How should investors approach bonds if they are worried that rates will rise further?

Mary Ellen Stanek: It depends on your objective. If you have near-term liquidity needs and you're more risk-averse, you don't have to take very much duration risk to earn relatively high yields. [Duration is a measure of a bond's interest-rate sensitivity that factors into its yield and maturity.] For longer-term investors, there is good value in bonds in the intermediate part of the [yield] curve. That is where our Baird Aggregate Bond fund and Baird Core Plus Bond fund durations are. They're in the high five-to-six-year duration range.

We are finally getting real yields after adjusting for inflation. In the third quarter, the Bloomberg U.S. Aggregate Bond Index's inflation-adjusted yield — the index yield minus the core Personal Consumption Expenditures price index — was 3.2%.

The Federal Reserve kept interest rates steady at its October meeting after raising rates in September for the first time in more than three years. What is the outlook for rates now?

I think rates will stay higher. It wasn't a surprise to see them on hold in October. We view that as more of a pause with a bias to another quarter-percentage-point hike later this year or early in 2027. It depends on crude oil prices and the inflation outlook.

Rates are attractive and are going to stay attractive. You don't want to run away from bonds, not at these valuations. The rhetoric out there can be pretty negative about volatility in the bond market.

Here's another way to look at it. At the end of the third quarter, the 10-year U.S. Treasury yield was 5.29% and the S&P 500 earnings yield, the reciprocal of the price-to-earnings ratio, was 3.81%. The last time the Treasury yield was that high was in 2002. This is a longer-term trend.

It is just another reason to at least pay attention to bonds and consider owning them.

What is your outlook for the economy?

The economy continues to surprise on the upside. Artificial-intelligence/data center spending has boosted gross domestic product readings, but consumer spending overall has also remained strong. We are concerned that the top 20% of U.S. consumers account for 60% of spending, while the bottom 80% account for 40%. If asset levels soften — that is, if stocks fall — and strong household net worth weakens, consumer spending could fall. But spending looks to remain pretty steady into 2027.

We are late in the credit cycle, but corporate-credit fundamentals are still solid, and strong flows into the bond market are keeping spreads [between corporate and Treasury yields] relatively tight. Spreads have widened a bit recently, as excessive optimism is softening with a bit of re-evaluation of market risk.

How are you managing portfolios to reflect your positive view on bonds?

We continue to think there is value in well-diversified, triple-B-rated exposure, and we are trying to keep duration generally more short to intermediate in the Aggregate Bond fund and Core Plus fund. In Core Plus, 27.3% of the portfolio is triple-B exposure versus the Bloomberg U.S. Universal Index's 13.1%. In the Aggregate Bond fund, it is 21.4% versus the Bloomberg U.S. Aggregate benchmark, which is at 11.5%.

In Core Plus, we are underweight below-investment-grade versus the benchmark. We don't think the value is as compelling there. In both funds, our weighting in financials is double that of the funds' respective indexes. There is good value in financials.

Which credits have you bought, and why?

We like Barclays Bank. It's a solid bank based in the United Kingdom, with a credit rating between high-triple-B and A, depending on the ratings agency. It has good earnings and capital. We bought five-year and 10-year bonds, with 10-years being the cheapest. The 10-year bonds yielded 1.43 percentage-point above U.S. Treasuries, an attractive spread.

Another name we like is Western & Southern Life Insurance. It is a high-quality life-insurance company, with a high-quality credit rating in the low-double-A range. We bought three-year funding-agreement-backed notes [bonds backed by insurance contracts] at a 0.65 percentage-point spread above the three-year Treasury. The notes rank at the policyholder level, a senior-ranking claim above ordinary corporate debt.

What is another favorite credit?

HCA Healthcare is the largest for-profit hospital chain and health system in the U.S., with its biggest footprint in Texas and Florida. We bought seven-year bonds, priced at a spread of 1.05 percentage points above the seven-year U.S. Treasury note. The credit rating is investment grade, mid-triple-B. [The debt] has durable demand in any economic cycle.

You are keen on municipal bonds. Why?

Munis have compelling value. Baird Municipal Bond fund has a yield of 4.86%. But the tax-adjusted yield is 8.21% for someone at the top tax rate of 40.8% [37% federal income tax plus the 3.8% net investment income tax]. An 8% tax-adjusted yield by historic standards is very attractive. Even for the Baird Short-Term Municipal Bond fund, which carries about a 21/2-year duration, yields at 4.12% imply a 6.96% tax-adjusted yield.

When you tax-adjust municipal bond yields, they are a particularly good relative value. We aren't saying that the equity market won't keep going [up], but [the bond market] is getting competitive for the marginal investment dollar.

What muni credits do you like?

Thematically, we have been trying to buy higher-quality issuers, those with longer call protection [the period when the issuer isn't allowed to redeem the bond early] to "lock in" yields for a longer time. We like general obligation bonds.

We like school districts. Warren Township Metropolitan School District in Indiana is one. The school district has an A-plus rating, and is part of the Indiana State Intercept Program, giving it an enhanced double-A-plus rating. [Under the program, the state will pay bondholders directly if the district is unable to, giving the bonds a higher rating.] The bonds maturing in July 2045 pay a 5.25% coupon and aren't callable until July 2036. The bonds were priced at $102.271 at new issue, and the yield to call was 4.95%. [Yield to call is the annualized return until the first call date and the payoff is the call price.]

How about another name?

The Alabama State Toll Road Bridge & Tunnel Authority has an Aa3/AA rating, with backing from the Alabama Transportation Department. We bought a 5.25% bond maturing in January 2051 and it is callable in January 2037. The bonds were priced at $100.942 at new issue and the yield to call was 5.13%. The proceeds help finance a bridge to replace an existing tunnel on Interstate 10 through Mobile, Ala.

Your early skepticism about data-center debt was prudent. What are your current thoughts?

Initially we were cautious because we thought the structures weren't in line with investors' interests. You have to look at each of the underlying credits to understand what the credit story looks like. You have to look at the structure of the security and do the obvious "what-if" scenarios. Not all of these projects are going to be successful. You want to make sure that you're disciplined about how you're getting exposure, and are you being paid to take it?

The AI buildout has been supporting the economy. What happens if that spending slows?

If it slows, it will probably be a gradual slowing, rather than something that stops suddenly. A gradual slowing could help with inflation or at least stop the rise in inflation.

The other thing to keep in mind is that the One Big Beautiful Bill Act allowed immediate expensing provisions for U.S. businesses. That was intentional. It was supposed to kick up economic activity and particularly a lot of capital projects to reshore production and bring supply chains to the U.S.

Anecdotally we have heard that the buildout is drawing in resources competitively, so if AI spending slows, will other capital project plans then take priority? Will the labor and resources just shift to some of those plans?

You have been a fixed-income investor for 47 years. Does the current environment remind you of anything else in your career?

I wouldn't say cycles repeat exactly, but there are patterns you recognize that give you conviction that you're on the right track directionally. In the past 15-20 years, below-normal interest rates fueled a lot of things, including a repricing of risk in some areas. Savers were hurt.

Now it is the opposite. We are starting to see strong demand for bonds. It is something we watch carefully because of all the debt that has been issued. We believe the strong demand is reflective of the value that investors see with nominal and real interest rates at attractive levels. Bonds are playing their traditional role.

Thanks, Mary Ellen.

data.title: How to Help Consumers: Credit-Card Rate Caps — Barron's
data.description:
By Randall W. Forsyth

Affordability, or the lack thereof, was the issue motivating voters in the midterm elections. Politicians clearly heard voters' voice but now comes the question of what to do about it. Energy prices are unlikely to come down soon to levels prevailing before the Iran war. Tariffs are unlikely to be reversed, and even if they were, it would do little to bring down the cost of housing or medical care.

But there is one price that can be lowered to bring relief to Americans' stressed budgets: credit card interest rates. "The cost of money is part of the cost of living," as an NBER working paper put it last year. Even though it's not counted in measures such as the consumer price index, the cost of credit has weighed heavily on consumer sentiment.

This is a rare issue that has support across the wide political divide in Washington. Sen. Elizabeth Warren, the Massachusetts Democrat who is likely to head the Senate Finance Committee in the next session, said on CBS' Face the Nation this past Sunday that she was ready to work with President Donald Trump on his proposal to cap credit card interest rates at 10%.

With credit-card balances hitting a record $1.29 trillion in the third quarter, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, a cap on interest rates on plastic surely would resonate with a public now paying an average of 21.19% on an average balance of $6,678.

Not only are 20%-plus credit-card rates high absolutely, they are high relative to other market-determined interest rates. Two decades ago, when the Federal Reserve's federal funds target was over 5%, credit card rates averaged under 14%. Now, with the 3.88% midpoint of the Fed's target range for its policy rate, plastic costs half again as much as 20 years ago.

Critics contend capping credit-card rates will mean less credit for riskier borrowers with low credit scores. A New York Fed paper published this past June came to that conclusion.

Other analyses found capping card rates may mean a hit to banks' profit margins. Another New York Fed paper found credit-card lending generated a return on assets more than four times the banking sector's overall ROA.

These fat profit margins leave plenty of room to lower card rates without curtailing credit to lower-rated borrowers, according to a study last year by Brian Shearer, director of competition and regulatory policy at Vanderbilt University. In fact, the majority of revenue for banks issuing cards actually come from "interchange" fees paid by merchants.

Shearer estimated that rate ceilings of 10% (as proposed by Trump and backed by Warren) would save consumers $100 billion a year. The benefit would accrue mostly to those with lower FICO scores (under 600), although it may cut lending and reduce rewards. But card issuers also could cut expenses, especially advertising.

Alternatively, a 15% cap would save consumers an estimated $48 billion annually, with no expected adjustments to lending volumes or rewards. An 18% cap saves just $16 billion, with top-grade borrowers possibly actually paying more if all banks moved to the ceiling rate, Shearer concluded.

While it's a rare issue that garners support from both parties in today's highly partisan Washington, past proposals to cap credit card interest have drawn objections from the formidable banking lobby. Still, it's an issue for consumers and investors to watch in the new year.

Mickey Mouse's job is probably safe, but spare a thought for the thousands of Walt Disney employees on the wrong end of layoffs this year. At least investors have been doing well heading into Tuesday's fourth-quarter earnings report.

By George Glover

As harsh as it appears, slashing jobs has helped power the entertainment and theme park company's stock 29% higher since late March, to trade at just under $120 as of Thursday. Shares of Disney's rival Netflix are flat over the same period.

Pleasing investors has been a top priority for CEO Josh D'Amaro, who succeeded Bob Iger in March. He joined Disney nearly three decades ago and headed up Disney's experiences division from 2020 to 2026. He has hit the ground running thanks to the cost cuts, his grand plans for streaming, and a rock-solid parks business delivering about 60% of the company's profit.

Shares suffered a Tower of Terror-style plunge from February 2021 to December 2022, shedding half of their value due to concerns about Disney's TV networks, including sports channel ESPN. But former parks exec D'Amaro's strong start as CEO means the stock may finally be ready to rally. Should investors consider buying in?

Here's how he has done it.

Let's start with the layoffs. (The exact numbers aren't clear but are expected to be in the thousands.) D'Amaro has swung the ax at divisions including Pixar and ESPN since taking charge as he bids to streamline the sprawling company. Slashing expenses won't win him any internal popularity contests, but it's just what investors wanted.

"The stock has traded in a range for a really long time," Seaport Research Partners analyst David Joyce tells Barron's. Shares have been trapped at $79 to $120 since April 2022. "The market gave D'Amaro a couple of quarters to get comfortable, but now we've seen layoffs and head-count reductions, Disney is putting the profitability narrative into place."

The stock's recent rally isn't just about cost cuts. Price hikes and ad-supported plans have at last helped make Disney+ profitable, after years when the streaming platform lagged behind Netflix. Analysts polled by FactSet expect profit for Disney's entertainment division to grow by 21%, to $6.6 billion, over the next two years, with streaming more than offsetting declines in its linear TV businesses like ABC and ESPN.

D'Amaro, meanwhile, has big plans for streaming. He promised to go all-in on technology in a 3,000-word letter to shareholders back in May, laying out a plan to make Disney+ a one-stop shop where users can interact with all of the company's different businesses. The CEO wants to make the streaming service "more engaging, more personalized, and more central to how fans experience our brands." The vision is for users to be able to move seamlessly from old Disney movies to live sports broadcasts to park promotions, without ever leaving the platform.

Big swings are possible because Disney's experiences division, which covers parks and cruises, remains a reliable moneymaker. Even the Iran war hasn't dented demand — analysts estimate that operating income for the division rose 11%, to $11.1 billion, over the fiscal year ended in September.

Barron's drew up a to-do list for Disney back in January, and we'd give D'Amaro an A- if we were grading his time in charge so far. The new CEO has signaled that he'll accelerate streaming growth and build on parks' strong track record — but ESPN remains a worry. D'Amaro mentioned the sports cable channel 15 times in the letter to investors, without laying out a clear plan for how to offset cable losses.

But the good news is that Disney's legacy TV networks are no longer a Dumbo-size problem, largely because their profit has taken a beating over the past decade — and the market has given up trying to price them in. From 2022 to 2025, operating income for the TV division dropped to $2.96 billion from $8.52 billion.

"That should no longer be a reason for Disney to get punished," says Morningstar analyst Matt Dolgin. "It doesn't even matter anymore....This company shouldn't be trading on that at all."

He says a sum-of-the-parts model could value Disney at $155 a share, with the parks and cruises business worth $175 billion by itself. The company's total market cap stood at $207 billion as of Wednesday.

D'Amaro has already convinced investors that he has the magic touch. If the looming report tops the Street's expectations, shares will get the pixie dust they need to extend their strong recent run.

By Steven M. Sears

Artificial intelligence may destroy humanity, and data center opposition could decimate the AI ecosystem, but the Democrats who now control Congress are unlikely to severely impede progress. Even the most vehement protesters are likely to evolve their thinking.

AI is a national security concern, critical to the defense and advancement of America, and that almost certainly protects data centers from punitive legislation. AI also has the power to advance medicine and science and make the world a better place.

It is safe to assume Democrats and Republicans understand that weakening America's AI dominance benefits China and Russia. The respected, nonpartisan Congressional Research Service has explained that since at least 2020.

Despite campaign rodomontade and widespread protests, the new Democrat-controlled Congress will likely develop realistic data center legislation, rather than use its powers to stifle an important technology.

Investors should use current controversies — and all that will follow — to build positions that benefit from what will likely be a national data center policy that addresses concerns, including pollution and extreme water and electrical usage, without impeding the AI buildout.

The investor class abhors political challenges, but major innovations need regulatory frameworks that balance public and private good. A lawyer helping a private-equity firm with a South Carolina data center said he didn't understand why they wanted to build near a neighborhood rather than in nearby rural areas. He has a point.

Some states and areas will likely emerge as pro-data center, just as state and federal legislation should ultimately harmonize as controversies mature. Volatility in its many forms — political, social, and financial — will define the process and create many investment opportunities.

Even now, many data center stocks are stable, despite so many Prince Hamlet investors who are vacillating between AI's stunning promise and cost. Amazon.com, Meta Platforms, Microsoft, and Alphabet data center spending is either dismissed as the cost of business or as insanity. Still, the AI investment theme is here to stay.

Aggressive investors can consider Equinix. Third-quarter financial results were strong, and the data center company's guidance was robust. Equinix operates 282 data centers in 36 countries. More than 90% of revenue is recurring. The 50 largest customers generated 35% of recurring revenue in the third quarter. Less than 3% of recurring revenue over the past three years came from the largest customer.

While the company is dynamic, Equinix's stock and options trading aren't, and that requires creativity.

For every 100 Equinix shares that are bought, investors can sell a put and buy a call. The put sale pays you to buy more stock at a lower price, while the call increases in value as the stock advances.

Consider puts and calls that expire in one to two months, with strike prices that are within 5% of the stock price.

During the past 52 weeks, Equinix stock has ranged from $720.62 to $1,128.68. Shares are up about 37% this year, far more than the S&P 500 index, a fact that reinforces that data centers are far from dead despite the headlines and campaign rhetoric.

The data center investment is likely to be long-term rewarding but short-term trying, as it will take time for political and local controversies to find reasonable legislative expression.

Recommending data center investments, moreover, expresses a view that investors have overreacted and that wagers against AI and data centers are too pessimistic.

Still, a lot must fall into place. Data center supporters must become as effective as Chinese and Russian propagandists, who are surely using social media and other tools to influence American public opinion and politics.

America must win the AI race. Any other outcome endangers national security and global stability, and that's bad for everyone.

data.description:
BioNTech appears undervalued. Like Moderna, it could flip the current market narrative through oncology efforts. But that's hardly the only thing that can move the stock higher.

By Jacob Sonenshine

Moderna, once left for dead as a company that had no real business outside of a declining Covid vaccine operation, has seen its stock nearly quadruple since mid-August. After years of hoarding cash, it's investing in a vaccine that could prevent recurrence of melanoma and lung cancer. Millions of people have those types of cancer, and since insurers spend thousands per patient annually, revenue could total tens of billions. The total oncology industry brings in hundreds of billions yearly, according to Iqvia.

Enter BioNTech. The Mainz, Germany-based company had a surging Covid vaccine business which subsequently declined, has a stock price that lost the majority of its value from peaks, has almost $18 billion in net cash and equivalents, uses messenger RNA, and is investing in oncology. Sound familiar?

BioNTech has its own cancer pipeline that could spark significant gains for the stock. Even in the worst case scenario, it could become a special situation, undergoing wholesale changes that could unlock shareholder value. The company could be well over $30 billion soon, suggesting a $120 stock price, or a premium of about 37% from Wednesday's close of $87.65. The average analyst price target is $115.

The stock looks cheap on multiple levels. The first one that jumps out is its cash levels. Net cash comprises the vast majority of its $21.7 billion market capitalization. That's rare; most pharmaceutical companies have more debt than cash, and are currently valued on the basis that future cash flows will surge as new drugs come to market.

BioNTech's market cap — stripping out net cash — leaves just $3.7 billion worth of equity value from future cash flows, or 1.9 times the $1.8 billion in revenue analysts expect for the coming 12 months, according to FactSet. That's a significant discount to the State Street SPDR S&P Pharmaceuticals ETF's roughly four times sales.

So, any positive oncology pipeline developments would spark large stock gains. Adding a few billion or more of sales from new drugs would do the trick if the market assigns a normal, pharma-like multiple to those revenue.

That puts the company's over 25 oncology drug candidates in focus. They're between Phase 1 and Phase 3 trials. Many target rarer cancers, while others have wider oncology applications.

One is for pancreatic cancer. Over 500,000 people globally are diagnosed, according to the International Agency For Cancer Research, part of the World Health Organization. Phase 2 is under way.

The most important one is Pumitamig. An antibody rather than mRNA, it could treat multiple cancers; pancreatic, colorectal, liver, non-small cell lung, triple-negative breast cancer, among others. "This would be a significant product, if successful," says Canaccord analyst John Newman.

Pumitamig could prove lucrative with its reach — and more information about it is coming. BioNTech will present Phase 3 trial data for a Pumitamig candidate that aims to treat breast cancer and other types in 2027. BioNTech and its partner Bristol Myers Squibb would split the profit. (Bristol Myers is a Barron's Investor Circle stock pick.)

Pumitamig is key, partly because it won't fully compete with Moderna and Merck's cancer drug. That focuses on Melanoma and lung cancer, and while it has other applications, many don't interfere with Pumitamig's focus areas.

If the oncology pipeline doesn't bear fruit, the stock won't necessarily fall hard. The pipeline is essentially not reflected in the stock to begin with.

The main risk is the $1 billion-plus in annual cash burn from the over $2 billion research and development budget. Continued burn would reduce net cash, hurting the market cap. But cash burn would happen gradually, while other developments could support the stock.

Among those is the potential for an activist investor to come in. The market will first give management a chance on cancer, but activism isn't unthinkable if the pipeline falters after 2028 trial data.

To be sure, early private investor AT Impf GmbH, or Athos Family Office, owns 41% of the shares, while founder and departing CEO Ugur Sahin owns 16%. Both shareholders would have lots of voting power, should another shareholder push for change.

But maybe Sahin or Athos would vote in alignment with an activist for changes upon pipeline failures. After all, Sahin is leaving. Pharma veteran Guido Oelkers will replace him in February.

"One hundred percent — the activist part could absolutely happen," says Jeffrey Walch, Bernstein Research analyst. "Someone could accumulate a lot of shares."

That someone could push for slightly less R&D, or cash flow-producing acquisitions. Walch says that, while activism currently remains theoretical, it would likely include a push for yet another management change.

New management could pivot the pipeline away from oncology if it disappoints. The mRNA technology can help treat other diseases.

"Is there some activist that is upset with the trajectory of the company and they want to bring in a new management team who they think is a better drug developer? That, I think, is reasonable," says Walch.

Walch isn't alone.

"If they don't have Pumitamig, then they really need to find something else," says Morningstar analyst Jay Lee. "Get new management in — something along those lines probably needs to happen if Pumitamig is not it."

Another small probability is a buyout offer. One can only speculate, but battered stocks that haven't grown in recent years are often takeout candidates. BioNTech's mRNA could attract a bid from a pharmaceutical giant.

"It's not out of the realm of possibility," says John Newman, Canaccord analyst. "Is it possible at some point in the future maybe Bristol Myers takes a look at BioNTech? Sure."

Elsewhere, Pfizer partners with BioNTech for the Covid vaccine. Pfizer declined to comment. Bristol Myers didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.

To be clear, there are no rumors of a strategic buyer or activism. The analysts don't include these situations in their current theses. A couple of small shareholders have activist histories. We, at Barron's, pose these possibilities as conceivable if oncology disappoints.

A BioNTech spokesperson told Barron's that Athos and Sahin currently plan to remain shareholders.

The point: Shares are more than worth a bet, given the pipeline or a special situation.

3 Moves Retirees Can Make in a Jittery Market — Barron's
data.description:
By Elizabeth O'Brien

Calm markets can mask portfolio imbalances like fair weather hides flaws in your home's leaky foundation. But solid construction matters when it's stormy outside, and now is a good time to make sure your retirement account can withstand volatility.

On Nov. 5, the S&P 500 had its worst single-day decline since the "Liberation Day" crash of April 2025, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq entered correction territory on fears that Democrat's overwhelming win in the midterm elections would imperil the artificial-intelligence buildout. While shares have recovered somewhat, choppiness remains as Nvidia has come under scrutiny.

The company, whose chips power much of the AI economy, said it is investigating whether CEO Jensen Huang's admitted dalliance with an alleged Chinese spy endangered company secrets or national security. The government is also looking into the matter. Along with broader concerns about the AI trade, these investigations could hang over the stock market for some time.

"The one thing the market hates is uncertainty, and you can't get certainty about this any time soon," says David Bahnsen, chief investment officer of the Bahnsen Group in Newport Beach, Calif.

Here are some moves for jittery retirees to make right now.

Take Stock

Investors may be surprised at the extent of their tech exposure. Thirty-six percent of the S&P 500 is in information technology, with the so-called Magnificent Seven making up most of that. If you hold any individual tech stocks or tech-focused indices in addition, you've got an even more concentrated position in a relatively risky sector.

Tech has been a fantastic growth engine, but it's anyone's guess whether it will continue to power big gains. Some are optimistic: Challenges like the need for capital and the political landscape are speed bumps rather than roadblocks, said Ed Yardeni, president of Yardeni Research, in a recent webinar. "Fewer people get hurt if you drive slowly with speed bumps," Yardeni said.

More bearish investors fear that an AI slowdown could bring down the entire market — and the economy at large.

Diversify

Absent a high risk tolerance, you probably don't want more than half of your stock portfolio in the S&P 500. There are reasons beyond AI risk to diversify: Other asset classes have outperformed this year, and a portfolio focused on large-cap growth will miss the benefits of this rotation. For example, the Russell 2000 small-cap index is up about 13% this year, versus the S&P 500's 10%, while the Russell 1000 value index is up about 26%.

If you're overweight tech, consider trimming your position and plowing the proceeds into less-flashy areas of the market. Investors may be hesitant to lose out on the growth potential of a highflying stock, but that shouldn't be the primary concern.

"In retirement, the question isn't how much more a stock could earn," says Ryan Sterling, CEO at NerdWallet Wealth Partners. "It's whether your money is ready to pay for the life you planned." If the appreciated stock is in a taxable account, capital gains are something to manage, but taxes shouldn't drive the investment decision, Sterling says.

Consider Dividends

Dividend-paying stocks are another good candidate for your proceeds. They tend to have lower volatility than the broad market, are less correlated with AI, and can help buffer market swings while throwing off income. Bahnsen builds portfolios of dividend growers for his clients. Names he likes include Pepsi, with a 4.2% dividend yield, and Chevron, with 3.4%. Investors who don't want to buy individual stocks can get easy access through the ProShares S&P 500 Dividend Aristocrats exchange-traded fund, which yields about 2.3%.

Retirees with enough dividend income to meet their living expenses can sleep well at night even if the market sputters.

data.title: How Donald Trump and Jensen Huang Forged Their Powerful Alliance — WSJ
data.description:
By Amrith Ramkumar, Brian Schwartz, Alexander Ward and Rolfe Winkler

WASHINGTON — Many tech executives warned last year that a flurry of state laws creating new artificial-intelligence regulations threatened to set the U.S. back in the AI race, but it was Jensen Huang who helped spur President Trump to act.

During a meeting in the Oval Office late last year, the Nvidia chief executive told a small group including then-chief of staff Susie Wiles and White House AI adviser David Sacks that Trump needed to take action to prevent a burdensome patchwork, according to people familiar with the matter. Shortly afterward, Trump fired off a post on Truth Social and signed an executive order attacking states enacting AI rules.

That heavy influence is attracting fresh scrutiny following the president's decision to stand by the CEO despite multiple affairs. Lawmakers are seeking more information about what Trump knew about the relationship between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang, the Nvidia business partner suspected of working for Chinese intelligence, as well as the administration's failure to stop artificial-intelligence chips from going to China.

More than almost any CEO, Huang helped shape the president's AI strategy and was involved in chip deals and state visits all over the world.

"This entire episode demonstrates the dangers of personalizing policy decisions, especially when it comes to national security," said Aaron Bartnick, a White House tech policy official during the Biden administration.

The White House declined to comment on Trump's relationship with Huang.

From the first time they met in January 2025, the president was taken by Huang's charisma and success building the chip designer into the dominant player in its industry, people familiar with the matter said. Trump often referenced Huang's genius and role in keeping the U.S. ahead of China in the artificial-intelligence race, calling him at night to consult him on major policy decisions, they said.

Trump frequently overruled administration officials who raised concerns about Huang and didn't take action when top advisers circulated a classified memo this spring laying out worries that the CEO had a close relationship with an alleged Chinese intelligence source. At Huang's urging, he approved several deals to send Nvidia chips to China and other countries posing security concerns and enacted an industry-friendly AI strategy that has helped many of the companies Nvidia does business with. Nvidia in turn agreed to invest $500 billion in the U.S. to help build a domestic chip ecosystem, committed $25 million for the White House ballroom and lauded Trump's moves to slash red tape.

'Was the woman a spy?'

Administration officials are now racing to blame each other for not cracking down on chip deals involving executives like Alice Huang. Many are targeting Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, whose agency oversees export restrictions, while observers and lawmakers question the president's loyalty to the former CEO.

In addition to tracking Alice Huang, U.S. intelligence officials collected information on Chinese businesses and their leaders and through that process learned about their connections to Jensen Huang, people familiar with the matter said.

Jensen Huang met with business leaders and officials in China on his visits and associated with many Nvidia customers in Southeast Asia. Intelligence officials haven't definitively proven Alice Huang is a spy, the people said, but her position at Megaspeed — and Chinese industry's ties to Beijing's security state — worried U.S. intelligence officials about the possibility of her sharing Jensen Huang-related information to Chinese spy agencies.

Attempts to reach Alice Huang were unsuccessful.

Top Democrats are pursuing investigations into the Commerce Department's handling of chip exports as well as the relationship between Trump and Huang, asking the White House to preserve all communications between the two.

"It is not just an intelligence issue; it's also a potential corruption issue," Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D., Conn.) said earlier this week. "There needs to be a really penetrating, comprehensive investigation of all the possible compromises of our intelligence that may have occurred, but also... that Donald Trump is so high on the head of Nvidia, and now is potentially linked to intelligence compromises." Asked on TV personality Stephen A. Smith's podcast Thursday whether Huang should have stepped down, the president sighed, then said, "Well, the big thing is, 'Was the woman a spy?' And I don't know if that's been determined yet, but if the woman was a spy, yes," Trump said. "If the woman was not a spy, perhaps it would be different."

Trump said he spoke to Huang on Wednesday. "He's going through hell," the president said. "What he feels most badly about is his wife and family."

'Taking over the world'

When other top tech CEOs were standing behind Trump at his second inauguration in January 2025, Huang was noticeably absent. He hadn't spent much time in Washington during Trump's first term and had only become a titan in the industry over the past few years following the release of ChatGPT and other popular AI models that ran on Nvidia chips.

Later that month, Huang scored a meeting with the president at the White House after Trump's advisers told him about Nvidia's importance to the economy.

Once he learned more, Trump questioned how Nvidia could hold such a large share of the chip design market, wondering whether he could break up the company or create more competition, he said at a White House AI event in July 2025. "I found out it's not that easy in that business," the president said before asking Jensen to stand up in the front row of Mellon Auditorium surrounded by administration officials.

Trump took Huang to the Middle East in May on the first trip of his second term, and eventually agreed to let him send chips directly to China later in the year. Trump then took Huang to the U.K. in September 2025 as part of the global tour that turned the CEO into the industry's de facto diplomat. U.S. negotiators used the promise of Nvidia AI chips to help secure a preliminary peace deal last year with Armenia and Azerbaijan, one of several examples of so-called chip diplomacy.

"You're taking over the world," Trump told Huang during an event in the U.K.

Trump scooped up millions of dollars worth of Nvidia shares in his personal brokerage accounts since returning to office in 2025. At least a third of the companies backed by 1789 Capital, a venture firm where Donald Trump Jr. is a partner, have also secured investments from Nvidia, according to a Wall Street Journal analysis of their investment portfolios.

A 1789 spokeswoman said that the firm has never communicated about an investment with Nvidia, save for Reflection AI, in which the two co-led a funding round. She said that Trump Jr. isn't a member of the firm's investment committee and doesn't vote on how the firm allocates capital. The president doesn't pick or trade individual stocks and independent financial managers handle his portfolio, a White House spokesperson said.

Warning signs

By the spring, national security adviser Marco Rubio had overseen the drafting of a classified memo detailing salacious concerns that Alice Huang was suspected of being a Chinese spy. After Trump had been briefed verbally on Huang's ties to Alice Huang and found out the Nvidia CEO wasn't joining his trip to China, he asked the Nvidia CEO to meet Air Force One in Alaska, U.S. officials said.

Rubio briefed the president on the plane before they picked up Jensen Huang, according to people familiar with the matter. The New York Times previously reported on the trip details. In September, Jensen Huang and his wife were at the head table with other executives for Trump's state dinner with Chinese leader Xi Jinping.

Huang was on stage at a live taping of the "All-In" podcast in Los Angeles in September, when his phone rang. It was Trump, who wanted to talk about how recent hacks and concerns about AI models carrying out cyberattacks were "a hoax."

Before Trump could talk to the audience, Huang struggled to put him on speakerphone.

"The great thing about life is that Jensen can develop the most complex computer chip in the world that nobody can copy for 10 years, but he can't figure out how to put me on speaker," Trump said.

In early October, Trump presented Huang with the National Medal of Science, the nation's highest scientific honor, while praising Huang for putting America at the front of the AI race.

At the end of the ceremony with other tech executives, Trump met Huang's parents, who moved to the U.S. from Taiwan. Huang's mom has trouble walking, so Trump helped her off the stage. Huang took a photo with his parents while wearing his new medal following his last public appearance with Trump, later saying "it's their American dream." Exactly a month after the ceremony, Nvidia's board launched the investigation that helped lead to Huang's ouster.

data.title: California Voters Pass Ban on Wealth Taxes — WSJ
data.description:
By Paul Kiernan

California voters had a chance to impose the nation's first-ever tax on billionaires' assets. Instead, they voted to ban wealth taxes altogether.

A ballot initiative to prohibit new state taxes on personal property is set to pass, the Associated Press said late Friday. Known as Proposition 42, the measure was leading by a 2.6-point margin with an estimated 96% of votes counted following the Nov. 3 election, AP said.

The outcome represents a coup de grâce for the one-time, 5% tax on California billionaires' net assets that also appeared on the November ballot. Proposed by a healthcare-workers' union to offset looming Medicaid cuts, the billionaire tax, known as Proposition 40, fell short of the majority needed to pass, the AP said on Nov. 9.

Proposition 42 was one of several ballot measures funded by billionaires including Google co-founder Sergey Brin, venture capitalist John Doerr and Stripe co-founder Patrick Collison as part of a nearly $400 million effort to defeat the proposed wealth tax. It was one of two that garnered enough voter signatures to be placed on the ballot, but voters turned down the other measure.

These rival ballot initiatives contained language that would have conflicted with the billionaire tax. The countermeasures also forced the healthcare union to spend most of its available funds earlier this year gathering signatures. That left tax proponents with scant resources to rebut the billionaires' barrage of attack ads, text messages and mailers claiming that the levy was a step toward taxing ordinary Californians' retirement accounts.

Proposition 42 could make it harder for progressives to do something they've said remains on their agenda: taking another swing at taxing billionaires' wealth.

The newly passed initiative prohibits California from imposing new taxes on financial assets or other personal property, besides real estate. Since it will amend the state constitution, it presents a major hurdle for state lawmakers to tax wealth via legislation, should they ever wish to do so.

Still, thanks to California's robust allowances for direct democracy, Proposition 42 may not stop proponents from trying another wealth-tax ballot initiative.

Progressives say they learned important lessons in the failed California campaign and remain committed to taxing billionaires' wealth. The head of the healthcare union that proposed the California billionaire tax has already floated putting a similar measure on the ballot in 2028 if the Medicaid cuts remain in effect.

"Just as the billionaires amended the constitution to prevent a future wealth tax, the citizens of the state can amend the constitution to allow and impose one in a single constitutional amendment," said Robert "Perl" Perlmutter, a partner at San Francisco law firm Shute, Mihaly & Weinberger.

data.title: CRINKS nations wage sinister new cyber war on the West but rank behind India in shutdowns
data.description:
China, Russia, Iran and North Korea feature prominently in Western cyber threat assessments, but only two sit on Washington's terrorism list and all rank behind the world's biggest democracy on shutdowns

Western officials and security firms have taken to calling the four 'CRINK', a label that has spread as the four deepen their ties. The shorthand is handy but to some extent it also blurs three different kinds of disruption - sponsoring terrorism, attacking other countries' networks and cutting off one's own citizens - each measured by a different body with its own agenda. To add to the potential for confusion, there is no single official ranking covering all three.

Which state counts as the world's leading disruptor depends on the measure and on whose assessment is trusted. On hacking, the case against the four is broad, consistent and made by multiple governments.

On terrorism it rests on a unilateral American list that has moved with US political shifts.

On shutdowns the second-worst offender is a democracy - the world's biggest.

It must be borne in mind that almost every attribution comes from Western governments or Western security companies, and the accused outrightly and routinely reject them, so the safer formula is 'accused by the US of' rather than a flat statement of guilt.

The short, but political, list

Washington's list of state sponsors of terrorism now has three names: Cuba, Iran and North Korea. Syria was removed from the list on August 24, when Secretary of State Marco Rubio rescinded a determination dating from December 1979. The US delisted Damascus on the same day it announced a fresh round of sanctions on Iran.

The designation is an American instrument, not a UN tool, and its membership follows US diplomacy as closely as it follows actual conduct by the governments named. Iran has been on it since January 1984 and North Korea since November 2017, according to the State Department. Cuba's place is the most disputed.

The Obama administration took it off in 2015 during the thaw with Havana, and the first Trump administration put it back on January 12, 2021. Joe Biden's move to remove it again in January 2025 in more of an anti-Republican political move than anything else was reversed by Donald Trump within hours of his second inauguration.

'Drunk with arrogance, President Trump decides without reason that Cuba sponsors terrorism. He knows he is lying,' Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodriguez was reported as saying at the time.

Russia is not on the list, although European governments accuse Moscow of a campaign of sabotage and hybrid attacks across the continent.

French President Emmanuel Macron said in September that Russian hybrid operations were now aimed directly at France and ordered new protection for critical infrastructure and defence plants, Reuters reported. China is absent from the list too. India, in essence a de-facto US ally by way of its deep and extensive strategic partnership, accuses Pakistan of sponsoring cross-border terrorism, which Islamabad denies, and Pakistan is not listed either.

In short, regardless of threats to or claims made by nations close to the US, only Washington decides which countries make the list. In the case of Russia and China, the size of their economies and business links to the US means that they are all but guaranteed immunity any time discussions on whether or not to add to the list of state sponsors of terrorism comes up.

Where the consensus holds

Hacking is the one measure on which Western assessments line up. The US intelligence community's 2026 Annual Threat Assessment, published on March 18, names all four, along with criminal ransomware gangs, as states that will keep trying to break into US government, corporate and infrastructure networks to collect intelligence, prepare future disruption and make money.

'The IC assesses that China and Russia present the most persistent and active threats and are continuing R&D efforts,' then Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard said in her opening statement to the House intelligence committee on March 19.

Recorded Future, a US threat-intelligence company, describes the four in its 2026 State of Security report as the 'most capable and consistently active hostile state cyber actors' its researchers track, busier with quiet pre-positioning inside telecoms networks than with spectacular attacks.

One Chinese campaign it describes exploited unpatched Cisco devices in more than 100 countries. New Zealand's National Cyber Security Centre meanwhile tied state-sponsored activity in the country to all four in its 2026 threat report, and found China 'the most persistent and capable state actor undertaking cyber activity in New Zealand'. Some 23% of the incidents of potential national significance it handled in 2025/26 had suspected state links, and its leading judgement is that frontier AI will speed up the threat. Beijing in routine denial mode, told Wellington to stop spreading falsehoods, Reuters reported.

China's operations are largely espionage, and it is absorbing AI fastest: China-aligned groups 'leaned on AI at nearly every stage' in the first half of 2026, Trend Micro said in its own 1H26 APT report, from turning public exploit code into mass-scanning tools to an AI agent that ran its own reconnaissance inside a victim's network.

Russia's activity is bound up with its war in Ukraine and with sabotage; the New Zealand report notes that disruption of operational technology in the energy sectors of several countries over the past year has been attributed to Russian state actors.

Theft as a way to boost state finances

North Korea mostly steals. Its cryptocurrency heists in 2025 'probably stole $2bn, which is helping to fund the regime', according to the US assessment. Chainalysis, a blockchain analysis firm, put the North's 2025 haul at no less than $2.02bn, up 51% y/y and close to 60% of the more than $3.4bn stolen worldwide, lifting its cumulative take to about $6.75bn. The North pulls off larger thefts with fewer incidents, often by planting IT workers inside crypto firms to gain privileged access, and the $1.5bn taken from the Bybit exchange in February 2025 was the record until this year.

On October 29 hackers drained about $6.4bn from Binance, more than three times the North's 2025 total and to date the largest theft in crypto history, and Chainalysis and the FBI both blamed TraderTraitor, a North Korean group.

Binance said on November 12 that it had covered all customer losses. Kim Yo-jong, sister of leader Kim Jong-un, dismissed the FBI's finding as a 'grave political provocation'.

Cryptocurrency stolen by North Korea-linked hackers. The 2026 bar is the October 29 Binance theft alone. Source: Chainalysis. IntelliNews

Iran takes the war online

Iran's hacking, however, is the most closely tied to physical conflict, and since the US-Israeli strikes of February 28 its cyber front has reached Europe.

France blamed the Revolutionary Guards on November 9 for October attacks that overrode the temperature controls of refrigerators in hundreds of supermarkets nationwide, and Paris prosecutors are seeking arrest warrants for the head of an IRGC-linked cyber unit and his two deputies. 'It is an attack of unprecedented scale and unprecedented aggressiveness,' Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said.

Trend Micro found Iran-aligned groups mixing espionage with crime in 1H26, including attacks on internet-connected fuel-tank gauges at US sites.

The bigger worry though lies on the seabed. Fibre-optic cables carrying the Gulf's internet traffic run through the Strait of Hormuz, already one of the world's chokepoints for oil, and 17 more run through the Red Sea, Reuters reported in April. A few days later, Iranian state-linked media began publishing maps of Gulf cable routes and landing stations - on April 22 - and floated charging cable operators for passage through what Tehran calls its waters, turning Hormuz into a digital chokepoint as well.

Red Sea cables were cut in 2024 and 2025, and repair ships cannot work safely in either waterway at pesent. To date, no Iranian official has ever formally threatened to sever a cable, and no damage has been officially attributed to Tehran.

Shutdowns start at home

Internet shutdowns are a different kind of disruption: governments switching off their own citizens rather than attacking someone else's networks. Access Now's #KeepItOn report, published on March 31, counted a record 313 shutdowns in 52 countries in 2025, up from 304 in 2024 and 289 the year before. Myanmar led for the second year running with 95, 76 of them imposed by the military regime. India came second with 65, the highest of any democracy, ahead of Pakistan with 20 and Iran with 11.

Conflict was the leading trigger for a third year, behind 125 shutdowns in 14 countries, and satellite internet services were cut 14 times in seven countries, up from four in 2024.

Recorded internet shutdowns in 2025. Russia's figure is the STOP project count cited by Access Now. Source: Access Now. IntelliNews

Russia's count is the least reliable though and is potentially much higher. The STOP project catalogued 20 shutdowns, 17 at home and three in Ukraine, but Access Now says the true figure may run to hundreds or thousands of local disruptions. Regional mobile internet blackouts, imposed to blunt Ukrainian drone attacks, stayed close to record levels in 1H26, according to the Na Svyazi monitoring project. Iran throttled international access through its war and only approved a plan to restore pre-January connections on May 25.

Internet shutdowns recorded worldwide each year. Source: Access Now. IntelliNews

Laid side by side, the three measures produce three different lists. Iran and North Korea appear under both terrorism and hacking. China and Russia lead on hacking and information operations without carrying Washington's terrorism label. The governments that most often pull the plug on their own people are mostly elsewhere, in Myanmar, India and Pakistan.

CRINK fits the hacking data best, and North Korea's Binance haul and Iran's assault on French supermarket fridges point to a year in which the four will rank higher still, with the sharpest blows landing where there is money to steal or a war to wage. At home, the switch-offs are not easing either and India under Prime Minister Narendra Modi has a lot to answer for in terms of so frequently limiting internet access to almost one in five of the world's population.

data.title: FAA Lifts Nationwide Groundstop that Upended More Than 14,500 Flights— WSJ
data.description:
By Andrew Tangel, Alison Sider and Jacob Passy

The Federal Aviation Administration lifted a nationwide groundstop that halted departures for more than four hours Friday afternoon, according to government and industry officials.

The hourslong groundstop upended travel for hundreds of thousands of people and the disruption is likely to ripple for days. Airlines canceled close to 6,000 flights Friday and have already scrubbed nearly 1,000 more on Saturday. Hundreds of flights either turned back or diverted as airports became gridlocked with too many planes on the ground and not enough room to park.

The problem started late Friday afternoon. The FAA halted departures shortly before 4 p.m. ET, citing extraordinary circumstances and safety concerns.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy wrote on X that there had been a communication issue affecting multiple air route traffic-control centers, which handle high-altitude flights covering swaths of the country. "FAA technicians are investigating the issue," he wrote.

"What we have is an incredibly old air-traffic control system," Duffy said Friday in a press conference. Telecom routers "actually got overloaded with data," he said.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told reporters at the White House on Friday that "there's no reason for the public to be afraid or scared for your loved ones."

More than 4,500 U.S. flights had been canceled and more than 10,000 had been delayed as of Friday at 7:40 p.m. ET, according to FlightAware. Airlines also started scrubbing weekend flights, with hundreds more than canceled on Saturday.

Even with the departure lifted, airlines were preparing for a difficult reset. Diversions and canceled flights left planes and crew members out of place for their next flights. That could create cascading scheduling problems into the weekend.

At Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport, word quickly spread among travelers while ground traffic appeared to suddenly stop on the tarmac late Friday afternoon. By early evening, telecom issues at some FAA air-traffic facilities were coming back online, according to people familiar with the matter.

The outage appears to be affecting a telecommunications network overseen by L3Harris Technologies, according to people briefed on the matter. The network handles crucial radio frequencies that air-traffic controllers use to communicate with pilots, the people said. It wasn't immediately clear whether the outage also affected the radar feeds that controllers use to keep aircraft safely separated in the skies.

An L3Harris spokeswoman didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.

United Airlines said it is responding to the groundstop and will work with customers to get them to destinations once the issue is resolved. American said it expects its schedule to be disrupted for the rest of the day, depending how long the groundstop remains in place.

"It will be all hands on deck across American to get customers on their way as soon as possible when the FAA lifts this ground stop," American said in a statement.

Several airlines issued waivers to allow travelers to rebook flights without penalty. At some airports, including New York's LaGuardia, travelers whose flights were canceled had to wait in long lines to get their checked bags back before they could go home. At Newark Liberty International Airport in New Jersey, security lines were empty as people milled about checking their phones for updates.

John Sturino, a musician who plays the drums, said he is going to miss a percussion convention in Indianapolis because of the flight delay. The Brooklyn native said he had been waiting half an hour in line to cancel his flight at the Delta lounge desk in LaGuardia Airport and get a refund.

"It wasn't worth staying in the airport," he said.

Sara Garven, 66, was traveling with her husband home to Wisconsin from Sarasota, Fla., when the couple were stranded in Baltimore where they had a layover. Overhead announcements were being made roughly every 30 minutes, she said, but the information was no different from what was available online.

"Some are sprinkling the Friday the 13th component, which isn't really helping," she said. "Our main concern is just getting home safely."

This is the second time in recent years the FAA has taken the extraordinary step of halting all departures across the country.

In 2023, a nationwide groundstop was ordered amid an outage of the FAA's Notice to Airmen system, which provides critical information to pilots. That order lasted for two hours, contributing to more than 1,000 flight cancellations. Before that, the FAA had only taken that step on Sept. 11, 2001.

The nation's air-traffic control system has been beset by communications issues leading to radio and radar outages that have affected various FAA facilities in recent years. Earlier this year, flights at New York-area airports were halted when a contractor accidentally cut a fiber communications line in New Jersey.

Write to Andrew Tangel at andrew.tangel@wsj.com, Jacob Passy at jacob.passy@wsj.com and Alison Sider at alison.sider@wsj.com
